title: Americans' One-Year Inflation Expectations Hit 3.9%, Highest Since May 2023
excerpt: The New York Fed's September Survey of Consumer Expectations shows households bracing for faster price growth across gas, food, rent, medical care and college costs — keeping the central bank on track for another rate hike before year end.
body:
• Respondents to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's Survey of Consumer Expectations said they project inflation a year from now to hit 3.9% — the highest level since May 2023, up from August's forecast of 3.6%.
  • Inflation three years out is seen at 3.3%, up from 3.2%, while five-year expectations held steady at 3%. Households forecast future price increases for every category the survey tracks: gas, food, rent, medical care and college costs.
  • What it means for readers: the survey keeps the Federal Reserve on track for another rate increase before year end, which would keep mortgage, auto-loan and credit-card rates elevated into 2027 — while high-yield savings accounts stay attractive a while longer.
  • The report lands as the Fed debates its next move: officials raised the rate target to 3.75%–4% last month and investors see December as the most likely time for another hike.

The public's near-term expected path for inflation jumped in September to its highest level in more than three years, as households downgraded both their current and future financial outlooks, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said on Wednesday.

Respondents to the bank's latest Survey of Consumer Expectations said they project inflation a year from now to hit 3.9%, the highest reading since May 2023, up from August's forecast of 3.6%. Inflation three years from now is seen at 3.3% versus 3.2% in August, while expected inflation five years from now held steady at 3%.

Broad-based pessimism on prices

The deterioration in the inflation outlook was broad. Households forecast future price increases for all the categories the New York Fed tracks — gas, food, rent, medical care and college costs — underscoring how entrenched the affordability crunch has become.

The report tracks a souring national mood that lines up with other recent readings showing downbeat consumers in an economy still suffering from high and persistent inflation. It lands as pivotal midterm elections loom, with polls suggesting President Donald Trump and Republicans face a rough ride amid an ongoing affordability crisis that analysts tie in large part to their own policy actions.

According to many Fed officials, the main drivers of the current outsized inflation gains are the ongoing impact of the president's trade tariffs, the energy price surges caused by the war in the Middle East, and pressure from the frenzied pace of investment in the tech sector.

"I still think it's inflation" that's weighing on sentiment. "Once we get inflation back down to 2% and people don't have to worry about it getting worse, then they can start to heal from what they've experienced over the last five years."

— Neel Kashkari, President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

Context: a Fed still tightening

Faced with inflation that continues to outstrip the Fed's 2% goal, officials last month raised their interest rate target by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Officials also signaled they expect to raise rates again before year end, with investors eyeing the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting as the most likely time for action — a view reinforced after several key officials said last week that the central bank has time to weigh the data before acting again.

The Fed's own projections show inflation, measured by its preferred PCE price index, finishing 2026 at 3.7%, well above the 2% target, with the central bank not expecting to meet its goal until 2029.

A mixed picture beneath the gloom

The September survey was not uniformly bleak. Households downgraded their views of their current and future finances and marked down their ability to access credit, yet became less worried about missing a debt payment. The job market assessment actually improved: relative to August, respondents lowered expectations that the unemployment rate would be higher a year from now, downgraded their expectations of involuntary job loss, and grew more confident they could find work if they lost their current position.

Notably, households said they planned to increase future spending compared with August — the highest reading since May 2023. Economists often watch this combination closely: consumers expecting higher prices but spending anyway is precisely the dynamic that can keep inflation elevated.

What to watch

The next signal comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' inflation readings and the Fed's own internal debate ahead of December. For now, the message from American households is blunt: they do not believe the price pain is ending soon — and the central bank is hearing them.
